Quoting the Ghostty post: over the past month the author kept a journal marking an 'X' on every date a GitHub outage hurt his ability to work, and almost every day has an X. A commenter had assumed GitHub complaints were a theoretical inconvenience, but noted two hours down that day plus constant outages that month.

Commenter says it has been remarkable watching GitHub 'just crumble as an organization'. They point to the unofficial status page (mrshu.github.io/github-statuses) as 'a horrifying story', and argue inertia is the only reason people haven't left.

Ghostty's author says he cried writing the post about leaving GitHub. He says he truly loves GitHub and it has given him so much, but 'it's not what it used to be'. The team discussed leaving for months before making the final decision.

On where to go (Codeberg, self-hosted Forgejo, GitLab, sourcehut, tangled): GitHub was 'the git community' and leaving fractures it. You need accounts everywhere and can't easily discover neat projects.

Workaround suggestion: since the lock-in is issues, PRs and Actions rather than git itself, use git-bug alongside a move to another forge like Codeberg. It stores issues and PRs in git refs and offers two-way sync with many providers.
User says the writing was on the wall when Microsoft required logins to search code just 48 hours after the acquisition.

Counterpoint on reliability: the commenter remembers GitHub always having reliability issues in its early days. It and Twitter were famous Rails projects with notorious, constant outages around 2008/2009.

Long-time user never developed an emotional attachment to GitHub. They are annoyed it is proprietary software that structurally locks users in despite being built on git, and that it doesn't work in Iran because it obeys US sanctions.
User says they switched from GitHub to GitLab after the master-to-main default branch rename, which they saw as a sign of wrong company focus.

Complaint that GitHub creates a default 'main' branch on repo creation. Renaming it is a hassle, and if you don't, 'you will definitely try to push to master and then realize the mistake and push to main, every effing time.'

User doesn't mind master to main in essence and thinks 'main' is a better fit. But GitHub went 'way too far' by aggressively pushing devs to rename their local master branches, and they almost accidentally renamed a former client's branch.
Complaint: GitHub's search is 'so terribly bad'. It is simply more efficient to clone the repo and use plain old grep.
Developer worries Microsoft ownership hurts GitHub's neutrality: 'If I would compete with microsoft in a certain space, I would really think twice about relying on github.'
Paying customer asks GitHub to prioritize SaaS stability. Their dev team and infra get hit 'seemingly every week' by GitHub outages, which seem to correlate with new feature releases.
With 3 members, the plan did not automatically drop from 5 seats. They had to manually downgrade seats from 5 to 3 to get the bill down to $12/month.

Downgrading from paid to GitHub Free removes several features in private repos: protected branches, draft PRs, Pages, wikis, code owners, and multiple assignees. You also lose standard support, Actions minutes drop from 3,000 to 2,000, and package storage drops from 2GB to 500MB.
User says they've not historically been a big GitHub fan, but 'the pace of innovation since the MS acquisition is really impressive.'
User who spread repos across GitHub, GitLab and Bitbucket depending on group size or features says the free team plan lets them centralize everything on GitHub.
User moved to GitLab when GitHub changed pricing, because GitLab had free CI/CD 'well before Actions', and never looked back.
Commenter says the one thing that would make GitHub a better alternative to GitLab for teams is self-hosted runners for organizations.
